comments.why: Demonstrates controlled safe landing of a quadrotor with a failed motor.
comments.text: This isn't quite true. Cheap drones may not have this capability, but controlled, safe landings of quadrotors with a single failed motor have been demonstrated, see this ETH Zurich video from 2014: [VIDEO] Obviously there are still other single points of failure such as the battery or controller, but at this point there's no excuse for crash landing a commercial drone just because a single motor (or rotor) has failed.

comments.author: SolarNet
comments.story: SureFly –  a personal helicopter designed for safe and easy flight
comments.why: Shows a quadcopter staying controllable after losing an axis of control.
comments.text: Actually that's a benefit of the quad-copter design. It can sacrifice an axis of control in that situation (a "minor" one, like rotation about the gravity vector). In this case it would likely make the passengers sick, but it would still be able to fly in a controllable fashion. See this video: [VIDEO]

comments.author: rtkwe
comments.story: Beijing From Above, aka How I was police detained for flying a Quadcopter
comments.why: ETH Zurich flight test recovering from propeller loss.
comments.text: You can't pull autorotation with fixed pitch blades, at least not in any meaningful manner. Light quads can fall pretty slowly with pinwheeling motors but that's not actually autorotation. The way a helicopter is able to autorotate is to pull negative pitch, which spins the rotors using the fall energy of the copter, then shortly before crashing pulling back to positive pitch and using the still spinning blades to slow down to a controlled landing. For motor failure ETH Zurich has some research out there about recovering to normal(ish) flight after a prop loss. The quad goes into a pretty rapid spin but it's still controllable, link below to an outside the lab test. [VIDEO]
